text: Hi, I'm Sebastián. I'm an AI engineer at the Gran Telescopio Canarias, the largest optical telescope in the world, here on La Palma.
This is one of the best night skies on Earth.
And planning a good night under it is still surprisingly hard.
This is Roque Nights: an observing planner where you and your AI agent share the same instrument.
Not an API behind a page. One live sky map, two operators.
I open it in ChatGPT's browser, and the app registers fifteen WebMCP tools, eleven always live, right here in the page.
I paste one prompt: plan me a three-hour night, best night in the next two weeks, avoiding the Moon.
Watch the panel. The agent ranks the nights and picks September 13th: new Moon, nine hours of darkness.
And the sky map moves. The agent is pointing the dome at each target while I watch.
Now, the part I care about.
I tap the sky and mark Andromeda and the Pleiades as my favorites. No typing, just a gesture on the map.
I ask the agent to adjust the plan around my favorites.
It reads my gesture through describe_current_view
and proposes a new plan: a ghost plan.
Nothing is committed until I say so. I review it item by item, and confirm.
And best of all, the plan is portable. I switch the site to Mauna Kea, Hawaii: a very different telescope.
The app flags it immediately: this plan was built for a different sky.
The agent revalidates it, four kept, four moved, and I export it: JSON, calendar, or a shared link that carries the whole plan.
Everything runs in the browser. Zero servers. All the astronomy computed locally.
WebMCP made this possible: the agent doesn't scrape my interface. It uses the same instrument I do.
So this is Roque Nights. Plan the sky with your agent.
Open source, live now, and built from the Roque de los Muchachos, La Palma.
